rationale: The Parkinson diet menu lists walnut oil without grade, individual assignment or a rigidity-item result. Cold-pressed walnut oil improved climbing in a fly toxin model, which does not measure rigidity. The two records leave the clinical direction open. The recovered Three-City original groups walnut with rapeseed and soybean oils, and reports dementia incidence. The 2008 brief describes that same cohort and gives no rigidity estimate.

The Parkinson caffeine trial reported a six-week bradykinesia subscore improvement of −1.70 points (95% CI −3.10 to −0.31), with the limb-only interval crossing zero. Black-tea infusion chromatography gives a measured link at lower exposure than the capsule trial. The independent PPMI preprint found worse bradykinesia with habitual caffeinated coffee, a different product and nonrandomized long-term exposure. The longer capsule trial and direct tea cohorts give total motor or incidence results without an interpretable bradykinesia comparison. The short randomized comparison remains the most informative result on the exact symptom and supports a limited easing lean. A matched, brewed-black-tea Parkinson trial remains open. The recovered 2015 Parkinson gut–brain review refers to the already counted Singapore incidence cohort. The review supplies no separate brewed-tea bradykinesia comparison. The independent Finnish cohort gives imprecise total motor estimates for coffee and diary caffeine, with no separate bradykinesia report.

Mouse studies use seed extract or fresh leaves incorporated into dried chow and measure memory tasks. The food composition study detects ergothioneine in freeze-dried basil leaf powder. The distinct isolated-compound pilot studied verbal learning in people with mild cognitive impairment. No comparison connects dried culinary basil with Parkinson executive function. Earlier external searches and cultural checks add ingredient-level context. A placebo-controlled healthy-volunteer study reports improved Stroop interference performance with an ethanolic extract of holy basil. This different species and exposure leave the direction for dried sweet basil in Parkinson disease open.

Dietary cold-pressed walnut oil improved climbing in a toxin-exposed fly study. A Parkinson diet menu contains walnut oil but gives only aggregate motor scores. Neither supplies a human oil-specific bradykinesia estimate. The original Three-City cohort adds a grouped walnut, rapeseed and soybean oil exposure and a dementia endpoint. The secondary news account adds no separate cohort or Parkinson bradykinesia assessment.

The age-adjusted plasma ALA correlation favored less rigidity, with a weaker sex-adjusted result. A combined-regimen narrative described improvement. The two flaxseed omega-3 plus vitamin E trials give aggregate results and omit a separate rigidity estimate. The first trial’s registry changed dose and outcomes after publication. No contrast isolates cold-pressed flaxseed oil. The 2008 news brief mentions flaxseed oil in a summary of dementia incidence. The cohort defined its measured oil group as colza, walnut and soybean oils and gives no flaxseed rigidity estimate.

No controlled or statistically clear evidence links cold-pressed flaxseed oil to bradykinesia severity. In early Parkinson disease (PMID34127758), plasma alpha-linolenic acid was non-significantly correlated with examiner-rated body bradykinesia (age-adjusted p=.171, sex-adjusted p=.372) and did not track dietary intake. Flaxseed omega-3 plus vitamin E trials (PMID28342967, PMID30554092) combined vitamin E, lacked isolated bradykinesia items, and reported inconclusive UPDRS Part III, while older-adult FAB motor series (p=.140) and rat activity (p=.595) were null and isolated-ALA animal tasks do not transfer. The claim therefore moves from legacy 51 to open. The 2008 news brief names flaxseed oil, while the underlying cohort defines an oil group of colza, walnut and soybean. That cohort supplies no flaxseed exposure estimate or Parkinson bradykinesia endpoint.
